learningObjectives.title: Costs, scale of production and break-even

questions.q: Which method of production is used to make single, unique or one-off items to a customer's specific requirements?
options: Job production
Batch production
Flow production
Mass production
questions.explain: Job production makes one item at a time, often bespoke, such as a wedding cake or a bridge.

questions.q: What does 'productivity' measure?
options: The output produced per worker in a given time period
The total number of products a business sells
The total cost of producing all output
The profit made on each unit sold
questions.explain: Productivity measures the efficiency of production, typically as output per worker or per machine over time.

questions.q: In lean production, what does the abbreviation 'JIT' stand for?
options: Just In Time
Job In Turn
Joint Inventory Total
Just In Total
questions.explain: Just In Time inventory management means materials arrive exactly when needed, reducing storage costs and waste.

questions.q: Which statement best describes flow production?
options: Continuous production of large quantities of identical, standardised products
Producing a group of similar items before switching to another product
Making single customised items for individual customers
Producing small quantities of handmade luxury goods
questions.explain: Flow production runs continuously along an assembly line to make many identical items at low unit cost.

questions.q: A factory has 5 workers who together produce 200 units in one day. What is the productivity per worker?
options: 40 units per worker
1000 units per worker
195 units per worker
205 units per worker
questions.explain: Productivity per worker = total output / number of workers = 200 / 5 = 40 units.

questions.q: What is the main aim of lean production?
options: To minimise waste of resources and time
To maximise the number of workers employed
To increase the amount of inventory held
To raise the selling price of products
questions.explain: Lean production focuses on cutting waste of materials, time and effort to improve efficiency.

questions.q: Why might a bakery choose batch production rather than flow production?
options: It can make different varieties of product using the same equipment
It never needs to clean or reset its machinery
It produces one continuous identical product with no changeover
It only ever makes a single unique item at a time
questions.explain: Batch production allows flexibility to switch between products, such as different bread types, between batches.

questions.q: Which of the following is a fixed cost?
options: Rent on a factory building
Raw materials used in production
Wages paid per unit produced
Packaging for each product
questions.explain: Fixed costs do not change with the level of output; rent stays the same whether output is high or low.

questions.q: What is a variable cost?
options: A cost that changes directly with the level of output
A cost that stays the same regardless of output
A cost that only occurs once when a business starts
A cost paid to shareholders as dividends
questions.explain: Variable costs, such as raw materials, rise and fall as the quantity produced changes.

questions.q: A business has fixed costs of $5000 and variable costs of $3 per unit. What is the total cost of producing 1000 units?
questions.explain: Total cost = fixed costs + total variable costs = 5000 + (3 x 1000) = 8000.

questions.q: A product sells for $20, has variable costs of $10 per unit, and the business has fixed costs of $10 000. What is the break-even level of output?
options: 1000 units
500 units
2000 units
333 units
questions.explain: Break-even = fixed costs / contribution per unit = 10 000 / (20 - 10) = 1000 units.

questions.q: How is contribution per unit calculated?
options: Selling price per unit minus variable cost per unit
Selling price per unit minus fixed cost per unit
Total revenue minus total cost
Fixed costs divided by number of units
questions.explain: Contribution per unit is the amount each unit contributes towards fixed costs and profit after covering its variable cost.

questions.q: What happens to average cost per unit when a business benefits from economies of scale?
options: Average cost per unit falls as output increases
Average cost per unit rises as output increases
Average cost per unit stays exactly the same
Fixed costs rise faster than output
questions.explain: Economies of scale, such as bulk buying, reduce the average cost of each unit as the firm produces more.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a diseconomy of scale?
options: Poor communication as the business becomes too large to manage
Buying raw materials in bulk at a discount
Being able to afford specialist managers
Borrowing money at lower interest rates
questions.explain: Diseconomies of scale raise average costs when a business grows too large, often due to weak communication and coordination.

questions.q: A business breaks even at 1000 units and is currently producing and selling 1500 units. What is its margin of safety?
options: 500 units
1500 units
1000 units
2500 units
questions.explain: Margin of safety = actual output - break-even output = 1500 - 1000 = 500 units.

questions.q: What does quality control mainly involve?
options: Inspecting and checking products for faults, usually at the end of production
Making every worker responsible for quality throughout production
Locating the business close to its customers
Reducing the variable cost of each product
questions.explain: Quality control relies on inspection to detect and remove faulty products before they reach customers.

questions.q: What is a key feature of Total Quality Management (TQM)?
options: Every worker is responsible for quality and aims to get it right first time
Only a separate inspection department checks the final products
Quality is only checked once products have been sold
Faulty goods are accepted as a normal part of production
questions.explain: TQM builds quality into every stage of production by making all employees responsible for it.

questions.q: Why is producing high-quality goods important for a business?
options: It builds a good reputation and reduces the cost of returns and waste
It always guarantees the lowest possible wages for workers
It removes the need to advertise the product
It means the business no longer needs any fixed costs
questions.explain: Good quality reduces wasted materials, returns and complaints while strengthening the firm's reputation.

questions.q: Why might a manufacturer choose to locate close to its supply of raw materials?
options: To reduce transport costs of bulky or heavy inputs
To be as far as possible from its workers
To increase the fixed cost of the business
To avoid having to buy any raw materials
questions.explain: Locating near raw materials cuts transport costs, which is especially important where inputs are heavy or bulky.

questions.q: Which factor might most strongly encourage a business to relocate production to another country?
options: Lower labour costs in the other country
Higher taxes in the other country
Fewer available workers abroad
Greater distance from raw materials
questions.explain: Lower wage costs abroad can reduce production costs, a common reason for locating operations overseas.
